nameStory: Mouse-ear cress gets its charming name from its small, fuzzy leaves that resemble tiny mouse ears when young. The soft, grayish-green leaves have a velvety texture that feels just like you'd imagine a mouse's ear would feel. It's also called thale cress, named after Johannes Thal, a 16th-century German physician who first described it.
description: Mouse-ear cress is a tiny annual plant that most people walk right past without noticing. This diminutive member of the mustard family rarely grows taller than 8 inches, forming a small rosette of soft, oval leaves at ground level. In spring, it sends up delicate stems topped with clusters of four-petaled white flowers so small they're barely noticeable. Despite its humble appearance, this little plant is actually famous in the scientific world as one of the most studied plants on Earth.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves covered in soft, star-shaped hairs that give them a fuzzy, grayish-green appearance. The basal leaves form a flat rosette and feel velvety to the touch, just like tiny mouse ears.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with four petals arranged in a cross pattern, typical of the mustard family. Each flower is only about 1/8 inch across and clusters at the top of thin, wiry stems.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a small, flat rosette of leaves at ground level, rarely exceeding 6-8 inches tall even when flowering. The entire plant could easily fit in your palm.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces narrow, upright seed pods called siliques that split open to release tiny seeds. The pods are about 1/2 inch long and stand erect on the flowering stems.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Flowering stems are thin, wiry, and often reddish, rising from the center of the leaf rosette. They feel delicate and can be easily bent between your fingers.

habitat: Look for mouse-ear cress in disturbed, sandy soils along roadsides, paths, and waste areas throughout New England. It thrives in poor, well-drained soils where other plants struggle, often growing in cracks in pavement or between stones. This adaptable little plant prefers sunny, open areas and is commonly found in gardens, parking lots, and anywhere the soil has been recently disturbed.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and form their characteristic fuzzy leaf rosettes. By late spring, tiny white flowers appear on thin stems rising from the center of each rosette.
seasonality.summer: Flowers continue blooming and develop into upright seed pods. The entire plant often completes its life cycle by midsummer in hot weather.
seasonality.fall: Seeds from spring plants may germinate to form new rosettes that will overwinter, as this species can behave as either a spring or winter annual.
seasonality.winter: Overwintering rosettes remain green and visible, hugging the ground with their soft, mouse-ear leaves pressed flat against the soil for protection.

funFact: This tiny, unremarkable-looking weed was the first plant to have its entire genetic code decoded and has been launched into space more than any other plant species! Scientists love mouse-ear cress because it grows quickly, takes up almost no space, and has helped unlock secrets about how all plants grow, flower, and respond to light.
confusionNotes: Mouse-ear cress can be confused with other small weedy plants in lawns and disturbed areas, but the combination of fuzzy, oval leaves in a flat rosette and tiny four-petaled white flowers is distinctive. Remember: if the leaves feel soft and velvety like mouse ears and the flowers have four petals in a cross, you've found mouse-ear cress.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "cress," mouse-ear cress isn't closely related to watercress or other edible cresses, so don't add it to your salad! While it's technically edible, it's quite bitter and not worth eating. The scientific name Arabidopsis means "resembling Arabis," another mustard family genus, while thaliana honors Johannes Thal.
compareHints: Mouse-ear cress differs from its relative lyreleaf rockcress by being much smaller and having simple, oval leaves rather than lobed or toothed ones. While lyreleaf rockcress grows on rocky cliffs and has more substantial white flowers, mouse-ear cress is a ground-hugging annual of disturbed soils with flowers so tiny they're barely visible. Both share the four-petaled white flowers typical of mustard family plants, but mouse-ear cress's fuzzy, mouse-ear leaves make it unmistakable.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its famous relative mouse-ear cress, lyreleaf rockcress has much more dramatically lobed leaves and tends to grow in rockier, more exposed habitats.
